content: [tt-mlir](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-mlir) is Tenstorrent's open-source MLIR compiler stack. It handles lowering from TTIR (their high-level ML IR) down to TTNN (their hardware runtime), making decisions along the way about [memory layout](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-mlir/blob/636a8c1f9a287970a9123c17fa473249978fd097/lib/Dialect/TTNN/Analysis/MemoryLayoutPropagation.cpp#L317), [how tensors are sharded across cores](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-mlir/blob/636a8c1f9a287970a9123c17fa473249978fd097/lib/Dialect/TTNN/Analysis/MemoryLayoutPropagation.cpp#L91-L97), and [tiling](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-mlir/blob/636a8c1f9a287970a9123c17fa473249978fd097/include/ttmlir/Dialect/TTNN/Types/Types.h#L12-L13). I've been wanting to get involved in a serious greenfield compiler project like `tt-mlir` for a little while, and scrolling through issues, I found a perfect, well-scoped ticket which happened to be unclaimed.

[Issue #8322](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-mlir/issues/8322) documents a crash. A Tenstorrent engineer filed it: compiling any operation on a rank-0 scalar tensor (e.g. a `tensor<f32>` with no dimensions, just a bare scalar value) blows up when optimization is enabled.

```
ttmlir-opt: /opt/ttmlir-toolchain/include/llvm/ADT/ArrayRef.h:157:
const T &llvm::ArrayRef<long>::back() const [T = long]:
Assertion `!empty()' failed.
```
The minimal case to get a repro was a scalar add:
The issue noted that at `optimization_level=0` the same program compiled and ran fine, and that the crash appeared at level 1 or above.

`ArrayRef::back()` is LLVM's bounds-checked accessor for the last element of an array. Calling it on an empty array hits a precondition assertion in debug builds, so somewhere in the optimizer something was calling `.back()` on a shape with no elements.

```
$ grep -rn "shape.back()" lib/Dialect/TTNN/ --include="*.cpp"
lib/Dialect/TTNN/Analysis/MemoryLayoutPropagation.cpp:781:      int64_t cols = (shape.back() + TILE_WIDTH - 1) / TILE_WIDTH;
lib/Dialect/TTNN/Analysis/MemoryLayoutPropagation.cpp:783:          (outputType.getNumElements() / shape.back() + TILE_HEIGHT - 1) /
lib/Dialect/TTNN/Transforms/Decomposition/DistributedRMSNormDecompositionRewritePattern.cpp:32:  if (shape[shape.size() - 2] != 32 || shape.back() % 32 != 0) ...
```

Two hits in `MemoryLayoutPropagation.cpp`, one in an unrelated decomposition pass. `MemoryLayoutPropagation` is an analysis pass that only runs under the optimizer, which immediately explained the level-dependent behavior. At level 0 the optimizer doesn't run, so this code never executes.
Both lines are inside `addReshardCandidates`:

```cpp
void MemoryLayoutPropagation::addReshardCandidates(
    std::vector<InputCandidate> &candidates, Operation *op, unsigned operandIdx,
    Value operand, TTNNLayoutAttr currentLayout, RankedTensorType tensorType,
    const llvm::SmallVector<BeamCandidate, 0> *producerBeam,
    Operation *producerOp, size_t resultIdx, size_t maxCandidates);
```

This function generates candidate memory layouts for each tensor operand in the compute graph. When the optimizer is deciding how to shard data across Tenstorrent cores, it calls this to enumerate possible resharding options for each edge. Tenstorrent hardware tiles tensors into 32x32 blocks (`TILE_HEIGHT = TILE_WIDTH = 32`), and a central heuristic in this function is `maxGridVolume`, a cap on how large a grid the reshard is allowed to target. The reasoning: if an output tensor has N tiles, sharding the input across more than N cores is wasteful because each core can produce at most one output tile.
Here's the full block that computes it:

`shape.back()` gets the last dimension, the column count in elements. For `tensor<64x128xf32>`, shape is `[64, 128]` and `shape.back()` is 128. For `tensor<f32>`, shape is `[]`. Calling `back()` on an empty `ArrayRef` is the assertion failure.
Once `maxGridVolume` is computed, it gets passed downstream to `generateReshardCandidates`, which uses it to filter out grids that are too large:
The crash happens before any of that filtering. It happens during the `maxGridVolume` computation itself, when the output is a scalar and `shape` is empty.
The fix is a guard added to the condition:

For rank-0 tensors, the block is skipped entirely and `maxGridVolume` stays at `std::numeric_limits<int64_t>::max()`, no cap applied. Scalar tensors don't have tiles, so the heuristic doesn't apply to them and leaving the cap unconstrained is the right behavior. The guard doesn't affect rank-1 tensors either: for those, `shape.back()` is the only dimension, and `getNumElements() / shape.back()` evaluates to 1, giving one tile-row. There's no `shape[rank-2]` access anywhere in the block.
The fix was the easy part. The test is where I got two assumptions corrected, one after the other.

The issue crashes at `optimization_level=1`. So I write the test at level 1. Obviously. Why would I test at a level the bug doesn't even appear at? I added `@scalar_add` to the existing `ttir_to_ttnn_pipeline.mlir` file:
My test passed. I was pleased with myself.

The reviewer came back with:

> *This test won't exercise your fix because you need optimization_level=2 to go through MemoryLayoutPropagation. Please transfer the test into test/ttmlir/Dialect/TTNN/optimizer/ and add a few more ops into the func so that reshard exploration is triggered.*

The test passed because the pass containing the crash never ran. I had written a test that would pass whether or not I'd fixed anything at all — a special kind of useless: the test that congratulates you for nothing.
That sent me to look at how the pipeline actually gates on optimization level. The relevant code is in `resolveOptimizationLevelOptions`:

`optimizerPassEnabled` gates at level 1. `memoryLayoutAnalysisEnabled` — what actually enables `MemoryLayoutPropagation` — gates at level 2. The issue's reproducer used a real system descriptor, which may enable different behavior at level 1. On the mock device, level 2 is what's required. None of that is in the issue; it lives in the people who built the pipeline.

On the hardware question: I told him I'd be happy to repro if I could get access to TT Cloud — quietly assuming this needed real silicon. It needed me to read his message more carefully. The crash reproduces on the mock device, as long as you're at level 2. I'd offered to source cloud compute about thirty seconds before I understood that.
I moved the test to a dedicated file, switched to `optimization_level=2`, and chained four scalar adds to give the reshard exploration enough edges to actually reach `addReshardCandidates`:

The `// REQUIRES: opmodel` directive means it only runs when the build includes the OpModel component (`-DTTMLIR_ENABLE_OPMODEL=ON`). CI builds without it. The two new lines in `MemoryLayoutPropagation.cpp` sit behind that flag and never execute in the coverage run. Codecov flagged 0% patch coverage. My instinct: noise, rerun. It wasn't transient. There was no rerun that was going to make it go away.

There was also the merge situation. My instinct when CI goes red for reasons that look unrelated to my diff is to hit rerun and hope. It usually works. What I didn't know: in this repo, each merge of `main` into a community contributor's branch re-triggers workflow approval requirements, meaning a maintainer has to manually re-approve CI runs every single time. I'd been merging `main` periodically to stay current — seemed like good hygiene — and quietly externalizing the cost onto him without knowing it. He asked me to stop. Fair. I'd been optimizing for my own tidiness.
To confirm the fix actually did anything, I checked out `main` into the cpp file and ran the test both ways:

```
$ git checkout main -- lib/Dialect/TTNN/Analysis/MemoryLayoutPropagation.cpp \
  && cmake --build build --target ttmlir-opt 2>&1 | tail -3 \
  && llvm-lit -av test/ttmlir/Dialect/TTNN/optimizer/scalar_tensor.mlir
Assertion `!empty()' failed.
Failed: 1 (100.00%)

$ git checkout fix/8322-rank-0-scalar-crash -- lib/Dialect/TTNN/Analysis/MemoryLayoutPropagation.cpp \
  && cmake --build build --target ttmlir-opt 2>&1 | tail -3 \
  && llvm-lit -av test/ttmlir/Dialect/TTNN/optimizer/scalar_tensor.mlir
Passed: 1 (100.00%)
```
The reviewer approved and the PR merged as squash commit `1ead25f` into `tenstorrent:main`.

The fix was four lines and took ten minutes. Everything else — which level runs which pass, why a passing test can be worthless, when to rerun CI and when to stop and explain — was codebase knowledge I didn't have and couldn't grep for. That's the part that doesn't transfer from your own projects. It's also, I think, most of what 'getting good at a codebase' actually is.
